loop.top3_why:
Candidate A uses a weighted combination with weights (w1) derived from a gradient‑boosted meta‑model trained on all other series in the run. Across the dataset this weighting scheme achieved the best mean validation score (0.6584) and, for this particular series, it outperforms the other two candidates on the two later validation windows (0.5493 vs 0.6545 and 0.6287 vs 0.6545). The series is strongly trend‑dominated with high predictability, and the diagnosis recommends a robust combination. The weighted scheme captures model strengths that are common across series, which is consistent with the trend‑dominated nature of the data. The per‑window stability of A (only the first window is identical to the others) indicates that it is not simply overfitting to a single window.

The other candidates are more generic: B is a plain mean, which is robust but ignores model differences and therefore performs slightly worse on the second and third windows. C uses inverse‑error weighting with shrinkage; while it is close to B, it does not provide the same level of performance on the later windows and may over‑emphasise models that happen to have low error on the training set.

Given the evidence that weighted w1 generalises well across the dataset and performs best on the majority of validation windows for this series, A is the safest choice for the blind test.
loop.top3_why_not: Candidate B (plain mean) is less discriminative and performs worse on windows 2 and 3, which are the most informative for a trend‑dominated series. Candidate C (inverse‑error weighting) is only marginally worse than B and risks over‑emphasising models with low error on the training set, which may not hold in the blind window. Both B and C lack the cross‑series learning that gives A its advantage and are therefore less likely to generalise as well as the weighted w1 approach.

Candidate A uses a weighted combination with weights (w1) derived from a gradient‑boosted meta‑model trained on all other series in the run. Across the dataset this weighting scheme achieved the best mean validation score (0.6584) and, for this particular series, it outperforms the other two candidates on the two later validation windows (0.5493 vs 0.6545 and 0.6287 vs 0.6545). The series is strongly trend‑dominated with high predictability, and the diagnosis recommends a robust combination. The weighted scheme captures model strengths that are common across series, which is consistent with the trend‑dominated nature of the data. The per‑window stability of A (only the first window is identical to the others) indicates that it is not simply overfitting to a single window.

The other candidates are more generic: B is a plain mean, which is robust but ignores model differences and therefore performs slightly worse on the second and third windows. C uses inverse‑error weighting with shrinkage; while it is close to B, it does not provide the same level of performance on the later windows and may over‑emphasise models that happen to have low error on the training set.

Given the evidence that weighted w1 generalises well across the dataset and performs best on the majority of validation windows for this series, A is the safest choice for the blind test.
